title: Medical Weight Loss Pricing
description: What to compare in medical weight loss pricing, including intake fees, recurring costs, medication inclusion, labs, and follow-up policies.
meta_title: Medical Weight Loss Pricing: What Programs Charge For
main_html:
Medical Weight Loss Pricing

Educational only. Not medical advice. No endorsements or rankings.

Quick answer

An advertised monthly price for a medical weight-loss programme is almost never the amount you will pay in month four. Three things move it: the medication is usually billed separately from the programme, the dose is designed to go up over the first months, and what is being dispensed at the cheap tier may not be the same product as at the expensive one.

So the question that actually compares two clinics is not "how much a month". It is: what does the first ninety days cost if everything goes normally, what exactly is the medication and who makes it, and what happens to the price when the dose increases.

What is actually being prescribed

Most of these programmes are built around GLP-1 receptor agonists — semaglutide and tirzepatide are the two names worth knowing — which are injected weekly and sold under different brand names depending on whether they are approved for weight management or for type 2 diabetes. A clinic may dispense the manufacturer's branded product, or a version put together by a compounding pharmacy.

That distinction is usually the single largest reason two quotes differ, and it is rarely stated on a pricing page. Compounded versions are not FDA-approved products and are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or manufacturing quality the way an approved drug is, and what compounders may lawfully prepare has shifted as the FDA's determinations about supply have changed. None of that makes a clinic disreputable — but it does mean "semaglutide" on two price lists can be two different things, and you are entitled to ask which one, from which pharmacy, before you compare the numbers.

  • Is this the manufacturer's branded product, or compounded? Which pharmacy prepares it?
  • Is the dose measured in milligrams of the same drug, or in units of a custom mixture?
  • If the product changes mid-programme, does the price change with it?

Why the price is designed to rise

These medications are started low and increased in steps, over roughly the first four to five months, to limit nausea and other gastrointestinal effects. Higher doses generally cost more. A programme quoted at its starting dose is quoting the cheapest month you will ever have, and a quote that stays flat across every dose is itself a thing to ask about — it usually means either the dose is capped or the cost is averaged, and both of those are worth knowing.

Ask for the price at each dose step, not the entry price. A clinic that cannot produce that table quickly does not have one.

What the fee should include, line by line

A programme that separates its lines is easier to compare than one quoting a single number. The lines that exist:

  • Intake and consultation — the first clinician visit, and whether it is refundable if you are not a candidate.
  • Laboratory work — typically a metabolic panel, A1c and lipids at baseline, sometimes thyroid function; and critically, how often they repeat.
  • The medication — separate or bundled, at which dose, and through whose pharmacy.
  • Supplies — needles, sharps disposal, shipping, cold-chain packaging.
  • Follow-up — how many visits, whether messaging between visits is included, and who answers a side-effect question at 9pm.
  • Refill management — who decides a dose increase, and whether that decision costs anything.

Ask for the full first-ninety-day total with everything included, in writing, at the dose you would actually reach. That one number is comparable between clinics; a monthly figure is not.

Insurance, and why it so often does not apply

Coverage for weight-management medication is inconsistent in a way that coverage for most other drugs is not. Many employer plans exclude obesity medications outright as a category, even while covering the same molecule when it is prescribed for type 2 diabetes. Where coverage does exist it usually comes with prior authorisation and documented clinical criteria — commonly a body mass index at or above 30, or at or above 27 with a weight-related condition — plus, on some plans, evidence of a documented attempt at lifestyle change first.

This is why so many of these programmes are priced for self-pay from the start. Manufacturers also run their own savings programmes and direct self-pay channels, and those prices move; a clinic's cash price is worth checking against them rather than assumed to be the floor. Ask the clinic to tell you plainly whether it will attempt a prior authorisation at all, because some do not, and that is a real difference in what you are buying.

Why pricing and safety connect

A cheaper programme is sometimes cheaper because the monitoring is thinner, and monitoring is most of what a clinician is for here. If a page will not say who reviews side effects, how a dose decision gets made, what happens if you develop persistent vomiting or signs of pancreatitis or gallbladder trouble, or how the programme coordinates with your own doctor, that is simultaneously a cost question and a safety question.

The cheap tier that removes clinician access has not removed the need for it. It has moved it to you.

Who should slow down on price-first shopping

If you have a complicated history — a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma, a history of pancreatitis, significant gastrointestinal disease, pregnancy or plans to become pregnant, or several medications that need coordinating — the lowest-priced option is unlikely to be the right decision path, because what you need most is the part the cheap tier removes. Pricing has to be read together with fit and follow-up, not before them.

The cost question nobody puts on the page

Weight lost on these medications tends to return after they are stopped, which is well documented and is the reason clinicians increasingly describe treatment as long-term rather than a course. That reframes the whole pricing question: the honest comparison is not the cost of three months, it is what this costs per year and whether you could sustain it if coverage changed or your income did.

So ask what happens financially if you pause, what happens if you stop, whether there is a maintenance tier at a lower dose and price, and whether any part of what you have paid for carries over.

Questions worth asking

  • What is the full first-90-day cost, at the dose I would actually reach, if everything goes normally?
  • What is the price at each dose step after that?
  • Is the medication branded or compounded, and which pharmacy prepares it?
  • Are labs included, and how often do they repeat?
  • Will you attempt a prior authorisation with my insurer, or is this self-pay only?
  • What support disappears if I choose the lowest tier, and who answers a side-effect question?
  • What happens financially if treatment needs to pause or stop, and is there a maintenance price?

Red flags

Watch for a single low number with no dose attached, no mention of labs, and no explanation of refill or follow-up logic — that pricing page is built for signups, not decisions. Be wary of a programme that will not name the pharmacy or say whether the product is compounded, of a quote that is flat across all doses with no explanation, of pressure to pay for several months up front before you know whether you tolerate the medication, and of any claim of a guaranteed amount of weight lost.

What to do next

Ask two or three clinics for the same thing in writing: the full ninety-day cost at a realistic dose, the price at each subsequent dose step, what the medication is and who makes it, and what follow-up is included. Then read those side by side with the weight-loss overview and your city page. You are comparing what each clinic includes over the first months and the first year — not whose first advertised number is lowest.
